rationales.D: Correct. Louis XVI called the Estates-General because the crown was nearly out of money. Once it met, Parisians argued over how much power the Third Estate should have.

questions.explanation: In June 1789 the deputies of the Third Estate were demanding that votes be counted by head. Paris followed every step. Pamphlets and speakers attacked the clergy and the nobles, and the king's officials did little to stop them.

questions.stem: Young's account would be most useful to a historian studying

options.A: how the royal court planned to respond to the demands of the Third Estate
options.B: how political writing and debate spread in Paris before the Revolution
options.C: how peasants in the provinces felt about the taxes and dues they paid to lords
options.D: how the clergy and nobility defended their privileges in pamphlets and speeches

rationales.A: Incorrect. Young was a visitor who stood in the crowds. He says the court took "not the least step," and he had no view of its private plans.
rationales.B: Correct. Young saw the pamphlet shops and coffee-houses himself and counted the new pamphlets day by day.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Young is in Paris. He mentions the provinces only in passing, with the words "they say."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Young says he could find only "two or three" works on that side worth knowing. His account tells us little about how the privileged orders made their case.

questions.explanation: Young counts the new pamphlets, describes crowds at the café doors, and notes the cheers for speakers. This makes his journal strong evidence of the political excitement in Paris in June 1789.

questions.stem: The "spirit" that Young says was being "raised among the people" contributed most directly to which of the following in July 1789?

options.A: the Tennis Court Oath sworn by deputies of the Third Estate
options.B: Louis XVI's dismissal of his popular finance minister, Necker
options.C: the storming of the Bastille by armed crowds in Paris
options.D: the National Assembly's decision to take over the Church's lands

rationales.A: Incorrect. The deputies took the Tennis Court Oath at Versailles on June 20, before July. It came from a quarrel inside the Estates-General, not from crowds in Paris.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The king chose to dismiss Necker on July 11. The news set off protests in Paris, so it was a cause of the unrest, not a result of it.
rationales.C: Correct. Parisians who had been stirred up by speeches at the Palais Royal seized weapons and attacked the royal fortress on July 14.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Assembly voted to take over Church lands in November 1789, not in July.

questions.explanation: On July 12, 1789, speakers at the Palais Royal called on Parisians to arm themselves after the king dismissed Necker. Two days later, crowds stormed the Bastille, a royal prison.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Burke treats liberties as an inheritance from the past, while Paine says each generation may decide its own government.
options.B: Burke defends rule by an absolute king, while Paine defends a monarchy whose powers are limited by a parliament.
options.C: Burke rejects the idea that society is a contract, while Paine builds his whole case on that idea.
options.D: Burke praises the reforms of the National Assembly, while Paine condemns them as too violent.

rationales.A: Correct. Burke calls English liberties "an entailed inheritance" from "our forefathers." Paine says "Every age and generation must be as free to act for itself" as the ones before it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Burke praises a crown that shares power with Parliament. Paine wanted no king at all.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Burke writes, "Society is, indeed, a contract," though he describes it as a contract between generations.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Burke attacked the National Assembly's reforms, and Paine defended them.

questions.explanation: Burke says rights are handed down like family property and should be kept, not remade. Paine answers that the dead have no right to bind the living.

questions.stem: Burke most likely wrote Source 1 in order to

options.A: persuade Louis XVI to give up his throne and leave France for his own safety
options.B: urge Parliament to give the vote to many more British men, as France had just done
options.C: warn British readers against following the example of the French revolutionaries
options.D: call on Britain to go to war to restore the power of Louis XVI

rationales.A: Incorrect. Burke defended the French monarchy. He did not want Louis XVI to give up the throne.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Burke warns against "innovation." He did not call for more British men to vote.
rationales.C: Correct. Burke wrote after some British radicals praised the French Revolution. He argues that Britain's liberties come from tradition, not from new theories.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Britain did not go to war with France until 1793. In 1790 Burke was arguing about ideas, not calling for war.

questions.explanation: Burke wrote in 1790, after a London minister named Richard Price praised the French Revolution in a sermon. Burke wanted Britons to value their old constitution. He warned that tearing down old institutions was dangerous.

questions.stem: Which of the following developments in France would Burke most likely have pointed to as support for his argument?

options.A: the French army's victory at Valmy, which turned back an invading Prussian army
options.B: the adoption of the metric system, which later spread across much of the world
options.C: the execution of the king and the mass arrests and killings of the Reign of Terror
options.D: the fall of Robespierre in 1794, which ended the Terror and freed many prisoners

rationales.A: Incorrect. A French victory showed the strength of the Revolution. It did not show the dangers Burke warned about.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The metric system was a new idea that worked and spread. It would not show that breaking with the past leads to disaster.
rationales.C: Correct. Burke warned that throwing away tradition would lead to disorder and tyranny. Bloodshed in 1793–1794 seemed to prove him right.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The end of the Terror was a step back from violence, so it would not support Burke's warnings.

questions.explanation: Burke said that a people who ignore their ancestors and build a state from theories will fall into chaos. Many readers later saw the Terror as proof that his warning had come true.

questions.stem: The ideas expressed in Source 1 most directly contributed to which of the following in the early 1800s?

options.A: the growth of liberalism, which called for written constitutions and free trade
options.B: the spread of utopian socialism, which planned new communities with shared property
options.C: the rise of nationalism that called on peoples to form new states of their own
options.D: the growth of conservatism, which defended tradition, religion, and slow change

rationales.A: Incorrect. Liberals drew more on ideas like Paine's. Burke distrusted rights based on theory rather than tradition.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Utopian socialists wanted to build new societies from a plan. Burke opposed remaking society by a plan.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Burke defended existing states and their traditions. He did not call for peoples to break away and form new nations.
rationales.D: Correct. Burke's defense of inherited institutions became a model for conservative leaders after 1815.

questions.explanation: Burke is often called the father of modern conservatism. After Napoleon fell, conservative leaders used ideas like his to defend kings, the Church, and the old social order.

questions.stem: The event shown in the painting is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Spanish monarchy's harsh response to peasant revolts against high taxes
options.B: Spanish resistance to French troops as Napoleon seized Spain's throne
options.C: a liberal revolt that forced the Spanish king to accept a constitution
options.D: the British army's capture of Madrid from French forces during the war

rationales.A: Incorrect. The men in the painting were not shot by Spain's own king. Goya shows the punishment of an uprising against foreign troops.
rationales.B: Correct. Spaniards in Madrid rose up against French troops on May 2, 1808. The next day, French firing squads shot many of them.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Liberal army officers forced Spain's king to accept a constitution in 1820, after the painting was made.
rationales.D: Incorrect. British forces did enter Madrid in 1812, but they did not shoot the people of the city.

questions.explanation: In 1808 French troops occupied Spain, and Napoleon forced Spain's royal family to give up the throne. Madrid rose up against the French on May 2, and French troops shot captured rebels the next day. In June Napoleon made his brother Joseph king. Goya painted the scene in 1814.

questions.stem: The style and subject of the painting most clearly reflect which artistic movement?

options.A: Neoclassicism, which showed calm, balanced scenes modeled on ancient Greece and Rome
options.B: Romanticism, which stressed strong emotion and the suffering of ordinary people
options.C: the Baroque style, which used grand scenes to glorify Catholic kings and saints
options.D: Realism, which showed the daily work of peasants and laborers in a plain way

rationales.A: Incorrect. Neoclassical painters such as Jacques-Louis David used calm, orderly scenes. This painting is dark and full of fear.
rationales.B: Correct. Goya fills the scene with darkness, blood, and terror. The man in white, with arms spread wide, draws the viewer's feelings toward the victims.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Baroque art was at its height in the 1600s and often honored rulers and saints. Goya shows unknown men being shot, not a glorious ruler.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Goya shows a terrible, dramatic moment, not everyday work. Realism grew later, in the middle of the 1800s.

questions.explanation: Romantic artists wanted to stir the viewer's emotions. Goya uses strong light and dark, horror, and sympathy for unnamed victims rather than heroes.

questions.stem: Resistance like that shown in the painting contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: a long war in Spain that drained Napoleon's armies and money
options.B: Napoleon's decision to give up the Continental System in order to win over Spain
options.C: France's conquest of Portugal, which became a French province by 1810
options.D: Britain's decision to make peace with France and pull its army out of Spain

rationales.A: Correct. Spanish guerrilla fighters and a British army tied down hundreds of thousands of French soldiers from 1808 to 1814.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Napoleon kept the Continental System until his empire fell. Spain's revolt did not make him drop it.
rationales.C: Incorrect. British and Portuguese forces held Portugal. The French were driven out by 1811.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Britain kept fighting in Spain. Its general, Wellington, drove the French out of Spain by 1814.

questions.explanation: Napoleon never crushed the Spanish revolt. The long war cost him soldiers and money that he needed elsewhere, such as in Russia in 1812.

questions.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data in the chart?

options.A: Britain paid back most of what it had borrowed within a few years after each war ended.
options.B: Britain's debt grew at a fairly steady rate from the 1690s to the 1810s.
options.C: Britain's debt rose most sharply in years of war and fell only a little in years of peace.
options.D: Britain borrowed more during the reign of Queen Anne than in any later period.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The debt fell by only about 10 million pounds from 1763 to 1775 and from 1784 to 1793, a small part of the total.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The bars jump in some periods and dip in others. The largest rise, after 1793, is far bigger than any earlier one.
rationales.C: Correct. The big jumps come in periods that included wars, such as 1727–1763, 1775–1784, and 1793–1817. In peacetime, such as 1763–1775, the debt fell only slightly.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The debt grew by about 38 million pounds under Anne, but by about 600 million pounds from 1793 to 1817.

questions.explanation: Britain paid for its wars by borrowing. The debt rose with each war against France and dipped a little in peacetime. The wars with revolutionary and Napoleonic France added the most.

questions.stem: Britain's ability to borrow such large sums is best explained by

options.A: lenders' trust in debts backed by Parliament and the Bank of England
options.B: large shipments of silver from mines in Britain's colonies in South America
options.C: the king's power to collect taxes without needing the consent of Parliament
options.D: the sale of lands taken from the Church of England during the 1700s

rationales.A: Correct. After 1689, Parliament approved taxes to pay interest on loans, and the Bank of England (1694) handled the debt. Lenders trusted that they would be repaid.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Britain had no silver-mining colonies in South America. Spain held the great silver mines.
rationales.C: Incorrect. After 1689, British kings could not tax without Parliament. Parliament's control made lenders trust the debt.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Church of England kept its lands in the 1700s. Its monasteries had been closed in the 1530s.

questions.explanation: Because Parliament stood behind the debt, investors were willing to lend to Britain at low interest. This let Britain spend far more on its navy and wars than its income alone allowed.

questions.stem: A historian could best use the chart to help explain which difference between Britain and France in the late 1700s?

options.A: Britain could keep borrowing for long wars, while war debts pushed the French monarchy into crisis.
options.B: Britain stayed at peace with France after 1763, while France fought costly wars against Austria.
options.C: British taxpayers paid less per person than the French, so Britain needed to borrow more.
options.D: Britain lost its Caribbean islands in 1783, while France won back Canada in North America.

rationales.A: Correct. Britain's debt kept growing without a collapse. France's debts from wars, including its help to the Americans, helped force Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Britain and France fought each other again from 1778 to 1783, and the chart shows Britain's debt rising in those years.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Britons actually paid more in taxes per person than the French. Parliament's taxes helped make British debt safe for lenders.
rationales.D: Incorrect. In 1783 Britain lost thirteen American colonies but kept Canada and nearly all its Caribbean islands. France did not win back Canada.

questions.explanation: Both countries borrowed heavily for war. Britain's lenders trusted Parliament, so it could keep borrowing. The French crown could not raise enough money, and its debt crisis helped start the Revolution.

questions.stem: The catechism was most likely intended to

options.A: prepare French Catholics to elect their own parish priests and bishops
options.B: persuade French Protestants and Jews to convert to the Catholic faith
options.C: teach French children that the Church should stay out of the state's affairs
options.D: use the restored Catholic Church to teach loyalty and obedience to Napoleon

rationales.A: Incorrect. Electing priests was part of the Civil Constitution of 1790. Under Napoleon's agreement with the pope, bishops were named by the government and approved by the pope.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Napoleon allowed Protestants and Jews to worship freely. The catechism is about duties to the emperor, not about converting others.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The catechism joins church and state. It says serving the emperor is serving God.
rationales.D: Correct. The catechism tells Catholics they owe the emperor "love, respect, obedience" and taxes, and that failing him is a sin.

questions.explanation: Children learned the catechism by heart in church. Putting duties to Napoleon into it let the government use the Church to teach obedience.

questions.stem: The catechism's claim that Napoleon acted "to reestablish the public worship of the holy religion of our fathers" most directly refers to

options.A: the Civil Constitution of the Clergy passed by the National Assembly
options.B: the festival of the Supreme Being led by Robespierre in 1794
options.C: the agreement Napoleon made with Pope Pius VII in 1801
options.D: the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes, which outlawed Protestant worship

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Civil Constitution of 1790 split the clergy and angered the pope. It did not restore peace with the Church.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Robespierre's festival honored a "Supreme Being," not the Catholic faith. It was part of the Revolution's break with the Church.
rationales.C: Correct. In the Concordat of 1801, the government recognized Catholicism as the religion of most French people, and churches reopened for public worship.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, more than a century before Napoleon.

questions.explanation: During the Revolution many churches were closed and priests were attacked. Napoleon made peace with the pope in the Concordat, which helped him win the support of French Catholics.

questions.stem: The catechism's explanation of why people owe duties to the emperor shows the most continuity with

options.A: the divine-right ideas used to support absolute kings such as Louis XIV
options.B: the social contract ideas of Enlightenment writers such as Rousseau
options.C: the Declaration of the Rights of Man's claim that power comes from the nation
options.D: Montesquieu's idea that power should be divided among separate branches

rationales.A: Correct. Like Louis XIV's supporters, the catechism says God himself chose the ruler and made him "his image upon earth."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Rousseau said power comes from the people's general will. The catechism says it comes from God.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Declaration of 1789 said power comes from the nation. The catechism says God "established him as our sovereign."
rationales.D: Incorrect. The catechism gives the emperor's power one source and asks for obedience to him. It says nothing about dividing power.

questions.explanation: Napoleon's officials based this lesson on a catechism written under Louis XIV. Though Napoleon came to power through the Revolution, he used the old idea that rulers are chosen by God.

questions.stem: Metternich's main argument in the passage is that

options.A: Europe's rulers should grant constitutions so that reformers will be satisfied
options.B: Europe's rulers should stand together to resist demands for political change
options.C: the great powers should end their alliance and each act on its own interests
options.D: religion should be kept out of politics so that the faith can stay pure

rationales.A: Incorrect. Metternich warns that concessions will "only further embolden" reformers.
rationales.B: Correct. Metternich wants governments to keep their institutions, silence reformers, and "strengthen their union."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Metternich wants the great monarchs to "strengthen their union," not end it.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Metternich wants rulers to defend religion against attack. He sees it as a support for order.

questions.explanation: Metternich believed that stability mattered more than change. He urged rulers to defend the old order together and to crush groups that wanted reform.

questions.stem: Metternich's concerns in the passage are best understood in the context of

options.A: fear that revolutionary ideas would spark new revolts against restored kings
options.B: fear that Napoleon would escape from the island of Elba and return to power in France
options.C: Russia's plans to take over the Habsburg lands in Italy and the Balkans
options.D: the spread of workers' parties calling for an end to private property

rationales.A: Correct. After 1815 the victors restored many old rulers. Metternich feared that liberal and nationalist groups, inspired by the French Revolution, would overthrow them.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Napoleon escaped from Elba in 1815 and was then sent to St. Helena, where he died in 1821. In 1820 he was no threat.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Metternich is writing to the tsar to strengthen their alliance. He is worried about revolution, not about Russia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Large socialist workers' movements came later in the 1800s. In 1820 Metternich feared liberals, nationalists, and secret societies.

questions.explanation: The French Revolution and Napoleon had overturned thrones across Europe. In 1820 new revolts broke out in Spain and Italy, and Metternich wanted the great powers to stop such movements before they spread.

questions.stem: Which of the following later developments would most directly challenge Metternich's claim that the union of the great monarchs "insures the political peace of Europe"?

options.A: the absence of a war among the great powers from 1815 until the 1850s
options.B: Austria's use of its army to put down a revolt in Naples in 1821
options.C: the Carlsbad Decrees, which put German universities under censorship
options.D: waves of revolution that spread across much of Europe in 1830 and 1848

rationales.A: Incorrect. A long peace among the great powers would support Metternich's claim, not challenge it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Crushing the Naples revolt is the kind of joint action Metternich wanted. It shows the system working as he planned.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Carlsbad Decrees silenced reformers, as Metternich urged. They fit his program.
rationales.D: Correct. Revolutions broke out in many countries in 1830 and again in 1848, showing that the alliance could not keep the peace inside Europe's states.

questions.explanation: Metternich's system kept the great powers from fighting one another for decades. But it could not stop liberal and nationalist revolts, which broke out across Europe in 1830 and 1848.

questions.stem: The ideas in the passage most directly reflect which development of the late 1700s and early 1800s?

options.A: the Enlightenment's confidence that reason could uncover the laws of society
options.B: Neoclassical writers' imitation of the balanced forms of Greek and Roman poets
options.C: the spread of the scientific method, with its careful observation and experiment
options.D: the Romantic movement's stress on emotion, nature, and common people

rationales.A: Incorrect. Wordsworth speaks of "the primary laws of our nature," but he means the laws of feeling, not rules found by reason.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Wordsworth wants plain language from common life, not polished forms copied from ancient poets.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Wordsworth is writing about poetry and feeling, not about experiments.
rationales.D: Correct. Wordsworth calls poetry "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings" and chooses "Low and rustic life" close to nature.

questions.explanation: Romantic writers turned away from the Enlightenment's stress on reason. Wordsworth looks for truth in feeling, nature, and the speech of ordinary country people.

questions.stem: Wordsworth's reference to "the great national events which are daily taking place" most likely refers to

options.A: the Act of Union that joined Great Britain and Ireland as one kingdom
options.B: Britain's long war against revolutionary France, which began in 1793
options.C: Parliament's long debate over ending the British slave trade
options.D: the spread of Methodist preaching in English villages and towns

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Act of Union was passed in 1800, but it was one law. Wordsworth means a steady stream of events that fed a hunger for exciting news.
rationales.B: Correct. In 1800 Britain had been at war with France for seven years. News of battles arrived constantly and was eagerly read.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The slave trade debate lasted for years, but it did not bring "daily" news that created a "craving for extraordinary incident."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Methodist preaching was a religious movement, not a series of "great national events."

questions.explanation: Britain fought France almost without a break from 1793 to 1815. Wordsworth worried that constant war news and crowded cities were dulling people's minds and feelings.

questions.stem: Wordsworth's view of feeling and nature is most similar to the ideas of

options.A: Rousseau, who praised natural feeling over the polished manners of society
options.B: Voltaire, who used reason and wit to attack religious enthusiasm
options.C: Newton, who described nature as a system run by mathematical laws
options.D: Adam Smith, who argued that free markets turn self-interest into public good

rationales.A: Correct. Rousseau taught that feeling and a simple life close to nature were better guides than refined society. Wordsworth praises rural life for the same reasons.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Voltaire trusted reason and mocked strong religious feeling. Wordsworth puts feeling first.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Newton saw nature as a machine that follows mathematical laws. Wordsworth sees nature as beautiful and a source of feeling.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Smith wrote about markets and trade. Wordsworth is writing about poetry, feeling, and nature.

questions.explanation: Rousseau said reason was not enough and praised feeling and nature. Romantic poets like Wordsworth took these ideas further.

questions.stem: Seeley's main argument in the passage is that

options.A: the wars between Britain and France in the 1700s were fought mainly over religion
options.B: the English conquered India mainly because their merchants wanted more trade there
options.C: France pulled ahead of Britain in both North America and India by the middle of the 1700s
options.D: Britain and France fought many wars in the 1700s mainly as rivals for empire overseas

rationales.A: Incorrect. Seeley explains the wars by the contest for the New World and India, not by religion.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Seeley says the English were moved "neither by ambition nor yet by mere desire to advance our trade," but by fear of the French.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Seeley says France had "the start" of Britain in India, but the wars he describes ended with Britain in control.
rationales.D: Correct. Seeley says Britain and France were "rival candidates for the possession of the New World" and competed in Asia too.

questions.explanation: Seeley sees the wars of the 1700s as one long fight, a "second Hundred Years' War." He says the real prize was empire in America and Asia.

questions.stem: The rivalry Seeley describes led most directly to which outcome in 1763?

options.A: France's gain of Louisiana and the Mississippi valley from the British
options.B: France's loss of Canada to Britain and of its power in India
options.C: the division of the Dutch trading empire in Asia between Britain and France
options.D: Spain's loss of its colonies in South America to the British navy

rationales.A: Incorrect. France gave up Louisiana in 1762–1763. The land west of the Mississippi went to Spain.
rationales.B: Correct. In the Treaty of Paris (1763), France gave up Canada to Britain. In India, France kept a few trading posts but lost its military power.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Dutch kept their trading empire in the East Indies. It was not divided in 1763.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Spain kept its South American colonies. It gave Florida to Britain but received Louisiana from France.

questions.explanation: The Seven Years' War ended in 1763 with Britain the leading colonial and naval power. France lost most of its empire in North America and its chance to control India.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support Seeley's explanation of why the English conquered India?

options.A: The East India Company earned large profits from the taxes it collected in Bengal after 1765.
options.B: British forces kept conquering Indian states long after French power in India had ended.
options.C: The East India Company often went to war with Indian rulers who had formed alliances with the French.
options.D: Britain's navy defeated a French fleet near the coast of France at Quiberon Bay in 1759.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Big profits from taxes would point to a desire for wealth, a motive Seeley plays down.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Wars that went on after the French threat was gone would weaken the claim that fear of France drove the conquest.
rationales.C: Correct. If the Company fought rulers because they were allied with France, that would fit Seeley's claim that the English acted out of "fear of the French."
rationales.D: Incorrect. This battle mattered in Europe and the Atlantic. It says nothing about why the English fought in India.

questions.explanation: Seeley claims the English were driven by "fear of the French." Evidence that British wars in India were aimed at France's Indian allies would back him up. Evidence of profit or of wars after the French were gone would cut against him.
